article_title: Chicago Classroom Demands for Authentic Intellectual Work
citation: Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka, and Fred M. Newmann. (2000). Chicago Classroom Demands for Authentic Intellectual Work: Trends from 1997-1999. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Analyze actual classroom assignments as a direct complement to standardized test scores when judging instructional improvement
description: Because high-stakes test score trends can improve for reasons unrelated to instruction, this report argues that collecting and scoring the assignments teachers give daily offers a direct window into instructional quality. As the authors put it, "These assignments—what teachers ask stu- dents to do on a day-to-day basis—are direct indica- tors of the quality of instruction." The principle was implemented by gathering typical and challenging writing and math assignments annually and scoring them against authenticity rubrics.
requirements: Teachers must submit both typical and challenging assignments, and a rubric-based scoring process with rater-bias adjustment is needed to produce comparable measures
constraints: Changes in the sample of schools over time and variable amounts of data from different teachers required statistical modeling to estimate trends
target_learners: elementary school students in grades three, six, and eight in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: quality of instruction in writing and mathematics
examples: The project collected 349 assignments from 74 teachers in 1997, 953 assignments from 116 teachers in 1998, and 715 assignments from 87 teachers in 1999, scoring them with many-facet Rasch measurement.
key_sources: Anthony S. Bryk, Jenny K. Nagaoka, and Fred M. Newmann. (2000). Chicago Classroom Demands for Authentic Intellectual Work: Trends from 1997-1999. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/chicago-classroom-demands-authentic-intellectual-work-trends-1997-1999

article_title: Parent Advisory Councils
citation: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org
title: Clearly define parent council roles and decision-making authority to engage and satisfy members
description: The brief recommends that sponsoring organizations co-design a shared understanding of a parent council's purpose among parents, educators, and administrators before the council operates. It argues that "Clearly outlining the council's responsibilities and decision-making authority will lead to more engaged and satisfied members," positioning role clarity as the foundation for effective councils.
requirements: Sponsoring organizations must co-design a shared understanding of the council's purpose among all stakeholders, including parents, educators, and administrators
target_learners: parents and caregivers serving on school parent councils
target_learning_goals: shared governance participation
informed contribution to school decision-making
examples: The brief directs policymakers to outline council responsibilities and decision-making authority as its first key takeaway for building better parent councils.
key_sources: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org

article_title: Post-Pandemic School Closure Trends: Schools Serving Black Students Disproportionately Closed
citation: Isaacs, J., Kuhfeld, M., Postell, S., & Hashim, A. (2025). Post-Pandemic School Closure Trends: Schools Serving Black Students Disproportionately Closed. NWEA White Paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Treat school closure decisions as equity issues, not race-neutral administrative acts
description: Because closures disproportionately affect schools serving Black and high-poverty students even after controlling for enrollment declines and poverty, the paper argues closure policy conversations must address racial discrimination. It concludes "school closures are indeed not 'race-neutral,'" and that district leaders seeking fair, transparent processes should confront these documented disparities when weighing which schools to close.
requirements: District closure analyses should examine racial composition and poverty alongside enrollment and fiscal data.
constraints: The paper's regression evidence covers the 2024-25 school year for traditional brick-and-mortar public schools in the 50 states and District of Columbia.
target_learners: Students in majority-Black and high-poverty schools facing potential closure
target_learning_goals: Equitable protection of educational continuity and community institutions during closure decisions
examples: The paper's logistic regression showed a 7.3% predicted closure rate for an entirely Black, high-poverty, 50%-enrollment-drop school versus 3.6% for an otherwise identical school with no Black students.
key_sources: Isaacs, J., Kuhfeld, M., Postell, S., & Hashim, A. (2025). Post-Pandemic School Closure Trends: Schools Serving Black Students Disproportionately Closed. article_title: Using Student Achievement Data to Support Instructional Decision Making
citation: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). title: Establish a clear vision for schoolwide data use with a data team and written plan
description: School leaders should establish a comprehensive plan for data use that takes into account multiple perspectives. Checklist actions are establishing "a schoolwide data team that sets the tone for ongoing data use", defining critical teaching and learning concepts, developing "a written plan that articulates activities, roles, and responsibilities", and providing ongoing data leadership. A written plan articulating activities, roles, and responsibilities
Ongoing data leadership

examples: The guide presents examples of written plans for achieving school-level goals

article_title: Del Norte Unified School District: "A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services through Project Cal-Well"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Del Norte Unified School District: A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services Through Project Cal-Well. https://www.wested.org/
title: Closed-loop referral system linking DNUSD wellness centers with community and county behavioral health providers
description: DNUSD established a closed-loop referral system with Project Cal-Well support after earlier referrals to community partners were often lost to waiting lists and lacked follow-up communication. The system "enables community-based service providers to refer students to the district's school-based wellness centers if they cannot meet their needs" and encourages regular communication with the county's Department of Behavioral Health, improving identification of unmet mental health needs in the district.
requirements: School-based wellness centers able to receive referrals
Regular communication between the district and county behavioral health
target_learners: Students needing behavioral health services beyond what community providers can supply
target_learning_goals: Access to school-based mental health services
Identification of unmet mental health needs
examples: Community providers unable to meet student needs refer them to district wellness centers

article_title: Humanizing Teacher Preparation: Claremont Graduate University's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812
title: Claremont Critical Social Justice Teaching Competencies and classroom ecology framework with nine domains
description: Claremont's Teacher Education Program uses its Critical Social Justice Teaching Competencies as the foundation for coursework and clinical programming, so that every assignment and class develops skills to interrupt deficit schooling. The framework centers relationships and interactions between and among students and teachers, emphasizing humanizing classroom experiences. The competencies explicitly address nine domains: "(1) philosophy of education, (2) pedagogy, (3) science of learning (data-driven instruction), (4) socio-emotional learning and experience, (5) funds of knowledge, (6) school climate and culture, (7) community and cultural wealth, (8) socio-political identity, and (9) worldview and global perspectives." Faculty operationalize the stance through concrete, observable teaching practices.
requirements: Competencies must be integrated into all courses, clinical observations, resident self-reflection, and evaluations rather than confined to one course
constraints: Applies to Claremont's own teacher preparation program; the report does not test the framework's effects experimentally
target_learners: teacher preparation candidates (residents) earning preliminary California credentials
target_learning_goals: critical social justice teaching practices
culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy
humanizing classroom relationships
examples: The program aligned clinical observations, resident self-reflection, and evaluations with the competencies and centered the work of diverse scholars as course texts
key_sources: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812

article_title: I code or AI code: A comparative evaluation of AI-rated scores in classroom observations
citation: Fong, Y., Xiang, J., Chan, T.-Y. D., Lee, K., & Lau, E. Y. H. (2026). I Code or AI Code: A Comparative Evaluation of AI-rated Scores in Classroom Observations. The Education University of Hong Kong. https://www.eduhk.hk
title: CLASS Pre-K framework: three domains of teacher-child interaction quality comprising ten rated dimensions
description: The Classroom Assessment Scoring System Pre-K is a standardized observational framework assessing classroom quality through teacher-child interactions. It comprises "three overarching domains derived from observed dimensions": Emotional Support (four dimensions including Positive Climate and Teacher Sensitivity), Classroom Organization (three dimensions including Behavior Management), and Instructional Support (three dimensions including Quality of Feedback). Dimensions are rated on a 7-point Likert scale from low to high quality, and domain scores are aggregated from dimension scores. In this study it served as the common framework against which human and AI ratings were compared.
requirements: Trained, calibrated raters (or an equivalently trained AI model) using the CLASS manual and exemplar videos are needed to produce reliable dimension scores
constraints: Footage of recess or unstructured free-play periods is excluded to maintain consistency with the measure's coding requirements
The CLASS methodology typically requires between four and seven observations per classroom for a representative classroom-level estimate
target_learning_goals: Quality of teacher-child interactions supporting children's learning and development
examples: The study applied the full CLASS framework to 87 video-recorded observations from 38 Hong Kong K1 classrooms, with eight trained human raters and a prompt-trained GPT-5.0 model scoring the same transcripts
key_sources: Fong, Y., Xiang, J., Chan, T.-Y. D., Lee, K., & Lau, E. Y. H. (2026). I Code or AI Code: A Comparative Evaluation of AI-rated Scores in Classroom Observations. The Education University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18274

article_title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
citation: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259
title: CLARA agentic analytics system
description: CLARA (Collaboration Literacy through Artifact Reasoning and Augmentation) is an agentic analytics system that transcribes discussions in real time, computes psycholinguistic metrics, and uses GPT-4.1 to generate concept maps and 7C collaboration assessments from transcripts. Artifacts are embedded with text-embedding-3-large and indexed into distinct ChromaDB collections, and a ReAct agent built with LangGraph and GPT-4.1-mini iteratively calls six tools (including search_sessions, get_concept_map, get_assessment, get_speaker_profile) to synthesize responses traceable to stored artifacts. Users can explore artifacts on a dashboard and constrain which artifact types the agent may consult.
requirements: Speech-to-text transcription with speaker attribution; artifacts indexed into separate vector database collections per artifact type
constraints: The collaboration assessment comparison relied on 10 discussions analyzed by human experts, which the authors state is not sufficient for strong generalizations
target_learners: Learners and educators in collaborative group-work settings, from workshops with child participants to college classroom discussions
target_learning_goals: Developing and assessing collaboration literacy
examples: The system was evaluated on a dataset of 12 sessions containing 35 discussions spanning technical debugging, policy analysis, generative AI, and exploratory science conversations
key_sources: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259

article_title: To Tab or Not to Tab: Measuring Critical Engagement in AI Code Completion Tools Using Behavioral Signals and Attention Checks
citation: Jessica Hutchison, Ian Tyler Applebaum, Kenneth Angelikas, Kush Rakesh Patel, Phuoc Nguyen, Antonio Lazaro, Nicholas Rucinski, Rahad Arman Nabid, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). To Tab or Not to Tab: Measuring Critical Engagement in AI Code Completion Tools Using Behavioral Signals and Attention Checks. Proceedings of the 31st ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3803400.3809394
title: Clover: an instrumented AI code completion tool with attention checks
description: Clover is a Visual Studio Code extension that uses the Gemini 3 Large Language Model to provide real-time, single-line code suggestions at the cursor position. It logs fine-grained interaction events (generation, acceptance, rejection, revision, execution) with timestamps, and deliberately injects attention checks: suggestions "semantically inconsistent with the student's immediate coding goal" whose acceptance or rejection probes critical engagement. It was designed to mirror GitHub Copilot's interface for ecological validity.
requirements: Implemented as a Visual Studio Code extension mirroring widely-adopted tools like GitHub Copilot to collect authentic behavioral data
constraints: Attention checks are deliberate deterministic incorrect suggestions and do not fully replicate spontaneous AI hallucinations in real-world coding
Relies on a single AI model, with significant differences in performance and latency based on model selection
target_learning_goals: Critical evaluation of AI-generated code suggestions during programming tasks
examples: Used in a 60-minute in-person lab with 55 students in a Java object-oriented programming course, with the rainfall problem as the task

article_title: CLARA: Can AI Assess Developmental Appropriateness in Children's Stories?
citation: Sijing Yin, Zirui Wang, Qian Liu, Jiamou Liu. (2026). CLARA: Can AI Assess Developmental Appropriateness in Children's Stories?. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05783
title: Bilingual benchmark of 1107 Chinese-English children's stories with silver developmental references and structured annotations
description: A benchmark resource of 1107 aligned Chinese-English children's stories extracted from storybooks and educational materials in PDF and PPT formats, with normalized silver developmental references and structured COG, LAN, and SEL annotations. The article states: "we construct a bilingual benchmark contain- ing 1107 Chinese–English children's stories col- lected from storybooks and educational materials in PDF and PPT formats." Manual verification of 100 sampled stories found 95% acceptable extraction quality, 93% correct story grouping, and 91% adequate bilingual semantic consistency; 1030 stories are retained for quantitative evaluation.
requirements: Aligned bilingual narrative text per story
Normalized silver developmental references mapped to five age groups
Structured annotations across COG, LAN, and SEL dimensions
constraints: Publisher age labels are noisy silver references rather than definitive developmental ground truth
English narratives are translations, so the design evaluates consistency under translation rather than cross-lingual or cross-cultural generalization
The 0-2 group contains only 30 stories and text-only analysis omits illustrations, repetition, and caregiver interaction
target_learners: Children ages 2-8 targeted by the collected stories
target_learning_goals: Developmental narrative understanding across cognitive, language, and social-emotional dimensions
examples: A story labeled 5-10 by the publisher is mapped to the 4-6, 6-8, and 8-12 developmental groups
A cloth-bear story is annotated with COG labels simple cause, action consequence, and routine understanding, with publisher reference 2-5 and CLARA prediction 4-6
key_sources: Sijing Yin, Zirui Wang, Qian Liu, Jiamou Liu. (2026). CLARA: Can AI Assess Developmental Appropriateness in Children's Stories?. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05783

article_title: Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions
citation: Li Siyan, Kai-Hui Liang, Shopnil Shahriar, Yilin Ye, Shiyoh Goetsu, Wei-Wei Du, Masahiro Yoshida, Tsunayuki Ohwa, Xuhai Xu, and Zhou Yu. (2026). Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641
title: Clinical Empathy Module for PA coaching chatbots
description: The Clinical Empathy Module is a pipeline attached to the Empathetic chatbot variant that identifies Empathy Opportunities in user messages and generates clinically informed empathetic responses. It consists of three submodules: an "Empathy Opportunity Classifier", a "Strategy Sampler", and an "Instruction Generator". The classifier is a GPT-4o-mini-based model with "a top-three classification accuracy of 85.3%"; the sampler draws from EO-specific strategy distributions built from statistics in Rey Velasco et al.; the generator produces system instructions for GPT-4o describing the chosen strategies. Only the Empathetic chatbot variant has access to this module.
requirements: A GPT-4o base model and WhatsApp/Twilio delivery infrastructure
EO-to-strategy mappings derived from the healthcare-professional response data of Rey Velasco et al.
Check-in questions designed to elicit negative self-disclosure so that naturalistic Empathy Opportunities arise
constraints: The module is not activated in the initial consultation session; it operates only in maintenance sessions
The chatbot does not retain every single past conversation, since summaries are condensed and only the top 3-5 relevant bullets are retrieved
target_learners: Inactive but motivated adults seeking to increase physical activity
target_learning_goals: Sustained physical activity behavior change
Increased intention to follow coaching advice and self-efficacy
examples: In the six-week study, the Empathetic chatbot using this module was associated with faster growth in intention to follow and self-efficacy compared to the Non-Empathetic condition

article_title: Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-Assisted Instruction
citation: Patel, K., Lin, Y.-Z., Raul, G., Shih, B. P.-J., Redondo, M. W., Latibari, B. S., Pacheco, J., Salehi, S., & Satam, P. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02998
title: CLaaS platform with integrated OCR-to-LLM instructional assistant
description: CLaaS (Cybersecurity Labs-as-a-Service) is an AWS cloud-based platform delivering browser-accessible cybersecurity labs via EC2 virtual machines, supporting tasks such as DDoS attacks, buffer overflows, packet sniffing, and ransomware attacks. This paper extends it with an "Instruction Simplification" button that captures the current slide as an image, extracts text with Tesseract OCR, and sends the raw text with a crafted prompt to an LLM (gpt-4) via API to generate a simplified, zero-shot explanation delivered in the CLaaS interface. Students rate the output on a 1-10 feedback scale stored for later analysis and prompt personalization.
requirements: An existing instructional slide deck within the lab platform whose content can be captured as images
API access to a general-purpose LLM and the Tesseract OCR tool
constraints: Operates in a zero-shot setting with no domain-specific fine-tuning or preprocessing
OCR introduces noise, particularly from UI screenshots and slide templates
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in university cybersecurity courses
target_learning_goals: comprehension of technical cybersecurity lab instructions and procedures
examples: Deployed in a live university course where 42 student ratings averaged 7.83; the OCR pipeline runs in production on CLaaS
key_sources: Patel, K., Lin, Y.-Z., Raul, G., Shih, B. P.-J., Redondo, M. W., Latibari, B. S., Pacheco, J., Salehi, S., & Satam, P. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02998

article_title: Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction
citation: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309
title: Eight learner-centered design criteria for classroom proof assistants, organized under learning and usability goals
description: The article proposes a framework of two broad goals — "learning: the tool should help students refine and improve their mathematical proof skills; and usability: the tool should not create unnecessary frictions in writing proofs" — expanded into eight numbered criteria: supporting active exploration, consistent model, requiring engagement, notation similar to written proofs, engagement similar to written proofs, easy setup, minimal training, and minimal tedium. The criteria were synthesized from prior classroom deployments and a workshop survey, and the authors believe they are transferable to classroom proof assistants for other domains.
requirements: The assistant must require genuine cognitive engagement with the mathematical ideas in order to complete exercises, and feedback should be provided for partial proofs, not just once a proof is complete.
constraints: The final two learning criteria apply specifically to settings where students are expected to write proofs on paper, since in many but not all classroom settings transfer to pen-and-paper is expected.
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate programming languages students
target_learning_goals: equational reasoning
structural induction
transfer of proof skills to pen-and-paper
examples: Criterion 5 motivated the major iteration between deployments: students had to explicitly write out evaluation steps instead of simply clicking possibly reducible sub-expressions.
key_sources: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309

article_title: An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training
citation: Hung-Yue Suen and Kuo-En Hung. (2026). An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2026.3693864
title: Closed-loop three-layer interpretable ITS architecture linking multimodal scoring, expressive diagnostics, and conversational coaching
description: The article proposes an ITS architecture that treats assessment not as an endpoint but as part of a closed loop of practice, feedback, and behavioral adjustment. It is "structured as a closed-loop feedback system with three distinct layers": a performance layer presenting Overall Rating and six BARS dimension scores, an emotion-aware expressive diagnosis layer treating audience-facing cues as behavioral signals, and a Conversational AI Tutor that resolves learner queries using retrieved analytic evidence. The design aims to move learners from performance awareness to interpretation to actionable change.
requirements: Rubric-aligned (BARS) annotated training data so scores trace to observable performance cues
A retrieval layer restricting tutor generation to the learner's own multimodal records
constraints: Asynchronous, upload-based design; no real-time feedback during live performance
Multimodal signals are summarized rather than modeled temporally
Adapting to a new rubric or domain requires re-annotation and retraining (cold-start dependency)
target_learners: adult learners and working professionals practicing on-camera oral presentation
target_learning_goals: on-camera oral presentation delivery and content skills
examples: In the 30-day field study, learners reviewed dashboard feedback and interacted with the AI tutor between pretest and posttest submissions, with additional evaluative uploads disabled to encourage distributed practice.

article_title: Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22
title: Use the five-cluster structure as a diagnostic framework for locating students' GenAI mental models and designing activities that stretch across cluster boundaries
description: The article recommends that faculty treat the five mental model clusters as a diagnostic framework: identify where individual students' mental models lie, then design learning activities that push thinking beyond that cluster. The authors write that faculty can use "the cluster structure as a diagnostic framework such as identifying where students' mental models lie and designing learning activities that stretch their thinking across cluster boundaries." The goal is an integrated mental model holding technical, educational, ethical, and governance dimensions as interdependent.
requirements: Faculty knowledge of the five-cluster taxonomy and a means of eliciting students' current mental models, such as concept mapping
constraints: Derived from a preliminary WIP study in one required technology ethics course at a single institution
target_learning_goals: integrated understanding of GenAI spanning technical, educational, ethical, and governance dimensions
examples: The authors suggest Cluster 1 students may benefit from human and societal context knowledge, while Cluster 2 students may need prompting to reflect on access, conditions, and risks

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: Closed-loop adaptive teaching assistance model integrating perception, evaluation, generation and feedback for music education
description: The article proposes an adaptive teaching assistance model for music education organized as a closed-loop path of "perception evaluation generation feedback". Student performance audio and multidimensional behavioral data build a big data repository; a multimodal contrastive learning transformer aligns audio features with symbolic music knowledge via cosine similarity loss; analysis results are mapped into a reward space; and the PPO algorithm fine-tunes generation parameters in real time so that output scores and accompaniments adapt to learner progress. The design forms "a reverse drive from evaluation to generation", establishing "an automated closed loop from monitoring to generation to intervention".
requirements: Performance audio capture and standard digital score input must be available so the CMT can align heterogeneous modalities in a shared high-dimensional space
The big data analysis module must quantify performance into reward signals and capability defect matrices to constrain the PPO generation policy
constraints: The article states educational statements should be interpreted within the scope of testing conditions and technical proxy indicators reported
The system was validated as a technical framework with the educational comparison serving as an auxiliary demonstration
target_learning_goals: instrumental performance skills in pitch, rhythm and dynamic control
personalized practice content matched to learner skill level
examples: In the 12-week quasi-experiment the experimental group used the adaptive system for real-time feedback and generated exercise tracks while the control group received traditional teacher-led verbal feedback

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: Cognitive load theory's cognitive architecture: working memory limits for novel information disappear for information retrieved from long-term memory
description: The review's foundational framework holds that novel information is processed by a capacity- and duration-limited working memory and then stored in an unlimited long-term memory. The article states that "Working memory was limited in capacity and duration when dealing with novel information but these limitations effectively disappeared when working memory dealt with information transferred from long-term memory." Instruction's major function is therefore to accumulate organised information in long-term memory, drawing on Ericsson and Kintsch's long-term working memory account.
requirements: Instruction presenting novel information must be organised to respect working memory limits
constraints: The limits apply to novel information; familiar information retrieved from long-term memory is not subject to them
target_learners: all learners acquiring novel, biologically secondary information
target_learning_goals: construction of knowledge in long-term memory
examples: The 1998 article's architecture, revisited here, grounded seven original cognitive load effects including the worked example and split-attention effects

article_title: Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review.
citation: Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2020). Testing (Quizzing) Boosts Classroom Learning: A Systematic and Meta-Analytic Review. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000309
title: Additional exposure, transfer-appropriate processing, and motivation theories account for the classroom testing effect; retrieval effort theory is not supported
description: The review evaluates four theoretical accounts of test-enhanced learning and concludes that "the research findings support the additional exposure, transfer-appropriate processing, and motivation theories to account for the classroom testing effect, but not the retrieval effort theory". Additional exposure attributes gains to reexposure of recalled material; transfer-appropriate processing to shared mental processes between quizzes and exams; motivation to enhanced effort, engagement, and test expectancy. The review stresses these accounts are "not necessarily mutually exclusive".
requirements: Moderator analyses linking effect sizes to control-condition reexposure, format consistency, and motivational indicators to adjudicate among the accounts
constraints: The review notes the retrieval effort prediction (recall tests beating recognition tests) was contradicted in classroom data, and that mechanisms proposed from laboratory research may have limited applicability to the classroom

target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of studied knowledge, concept comprehension, and knowledge application in problem solving
examples: The review cites Schrank (2016) finding daily-exam class attendance stayed near 90% across a semester while control attendance fell to about 66%, as motivational support

article_title: Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning
citation: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457
title: Rethinking cognitive load theory's assumptions in light of productive failure findings
description: The article argues cognitive load theory needs a rethink of two basic assumptions: that cognitive load is the main mechanism of learning, and that higher cognitive load is monotonically bad for learning. It states "It may also not always be true that the higher the cognitive load, the worse the learning," since higher load can drive attention and activate prior knowledge that helps students learn from instruction. Evidence from productive failure research shows the initial problem-solving phase engenders higher cognitive load yet leads to better learning from subsequent instruction. The article also argues CLT's definition of learning as schema acquisition is too narrow and its proponents have theoretically underdetermined CLT by assuming learners have no prior knowledge.
requirements: Consideration of cognitive, social, and cultural mechanisms alongside cognitive load, with the choice of mechanisms depending on learning goals
constraints: Kalyuga and Singh (2015) are cited as arguing CLT's recommendations may be limited to contexts where the instructional goal is schema acquisition of basic knowledge, not complex problem-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
transfer
prior knowledge activation
examples: The article cites Kalyuga et al. (2001) showing worked-example benefits disappeared as domain knowledge increased, and argues CLT allows but underresearches using unguided problem solving to activate learners' prior knowledge

article_title: Effects of a Classroom-Based Program on Physical Activity and On-Task Behavior
citation: Mahar, M. T., Murphy, S. K., Rowe, D. A., Golden, J., Shields, A. T., & Raedeke, T. D. (2006). Effects of a Classroom-Based Program on Physical Activity and On-Task Behavior. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 38(12), 2086-2094. https://doi.org/10.1249/01.mss.0000235359.16685.a3
title: Integrate short physical activity breaks into classroom instruction to raise physical activity and on-task behavior
description: The article supports embedding structured physical activity into the classroom day rather than relying only on recess or PE. Its conclusion states that "A classroom-based physical activity program was effective for increasing daily in-school physical activity and improving on-task behavior during academic instruction." Because the activity occurs in the classroom, it adds activity minutes without displacing academic instruction time.
requirements: Classroom teachers implement the activity program systematically during the school day
constraints: Evidence is from elementary school students; effects on other grade levels are not reported in this study

on-task behavior during academic instruction
examples: The study assigned 135 intervention students to receive Energizers and compared their in-school steps and on-task behavior with 108 control students.

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Classic theories: theories from external fields applied to explain aspects of implementation
description: Classic (or classic change) theories constitute the third category: theories originating from fields external to implementation science, such as psychology, sociology and organizational theory, applied to provide understanding and/or explanation of aspects of implementation. They are considered passive relative to action models because they "describe change mechanisms and explain how change occurs without ambitions to actually bring about change". Examples include the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Social Cognitive Theory, social network theories, communities of practice, organizational theories and the Theory of Diffusion.
requirements: Relevance to the determinant type being analysed, e.g. psychological theories for user/adopter characteristics and organizational theories for context
constraints: Organizational theories' actual use in empirical implementation studies is relatively limited despite increased interest
target_learning_goals: explaining determinants of implementation outcomes at individual, collective and organizational levels
examples: The Theory of Diffusion's innovation attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability) are widely applied in individual studies and determinant frameworks

citation: Orton, A. (1983). Students' understanding of integration. Educational Studies in Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00704699
title: Clinical interviewing method for probing students' calculus understanding
description: A clinical interviewing method in which students respond to calculus tasks while the researcher probes their reasoning, used here to investigate understanding of elementary calculus. article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Cognitive load theory's model of human cognitive architecture: limited working memory with modality-based subcomponents and an effectively unlimited long-term memory holding schemas
description: The article presents cognitive load theory as resting on a specific cognitive architecture. It assumes "a limited capacity working memory that includes partially independent subcomponents to deal with auditory/verbal material and visual/2- or 3-dimensional information" alongside "an effectively unlimited long-term memory, holding schemas that vary in their degree of automation." These structures are the basis from which the theory derives its instructional guidelines.
requirements: Instructional guidelines derived from the theory depend on the assumed architecture of limited working memory and schema-based long-term memory.

target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation

citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Sweller, J. (2005). Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 147–177 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-3951-0
title: Cognitive Load Theory grounded in an analogy between human cognitive architecture and biological evolution
description: The article frames Cognitive Load Theory by connecting the cognitive processes assumed by CLT to the processes used by biological evolution, strengthening the theory's cognitive base. As the abstract states, the article "strengthens the cognitive base of CLT by linking cognitive processes to the processes used by biological evolution." This evolutionary analogy serves as the theoretical foundation for the instructional-design developments the review then discusses.

citation: Burin, D. I., Irrazabal, N., Injoque Ricle, I., Saux, G., & Barreyro, J. P. (2018). Self-reported internet skills, previous knowledge and working memory in text comprehension in E-learning. They recommend that teachers and instructional designers consider this before implementing the common practice of closed-question comprehension checks after lessons.

citation: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052
title: Classroom Video Analysis (CVA) assessment of teachers' usable mathematical teaching knowledge
description: The CVA is a video-based instrument that "elicits usable teaching knowledge by asking teachers to analyze teaching episodes shown in video clips of authentic mathematics instruction." Teachers' written responses are scored by trained raters and machine learning techniques according to four rubrics: analysis of the mathematics, analysis of student thinking, suggestions for improvement, and overall depth of interpretation, each scored 0–2. The study used a short three-clip version on variables, expressions, and equations, with internal consistency α = .82 for rater-assigned rubric scores.

constraints: The study used only three video clips selected for psychometric functioning, a short version of the full scale

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Cognitive load theory (redundancy effect) and cognitive theory of multimedia learning (coherence principle) as the account predicting agent dimensionality effects
description: The article uses cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning as explanatory frameworks for pedagogical agent design. It states that the observed dimensionality difference came "As predicted by the redundancy effect of cognitive load theory and the coherence principle of cognitive theory of multimedia learning". Under these frameworks, adding a 3D agent introduces redundant or extraneous material that the coherence principle and redundancy effect predict will hinder learning, explaining why simpler 2D agents tended to yield larger effects.
requirements: Applies to multimedia learning environments in which an on-screen agent's visual complexity could act as redundant or extraneous material.
constraints: The article presents this account as a prediction confirmed for the 2D-versus-3D contrast, hedged as a tendency rather than a decisive test.
target_learning_goals: Multimedia learning outcomes (retention and understanding of instructional content)
examples: The meta-analysis compared pooled effects for 2D agents (g+ = 0.38) and 3D agents (g+ = 0.11) and interpreted the difference through these two frameworks.

title: Clarify conceptions of communication, collaboration, and learning before designing computer support for collaborative learning
description: The article's foundational design principle is that technology design for collaborative learning cannot proceed without conceptual clarity. As it puts it, 'We cannot really understand how to create computer support for collaborative learning without first becoming clearer about what we mean by communication, collaboration, and learning.' The principle directs designers and researchers to settle their theoretical commitments about these three constructs before building or evaluating systems, because implicit conceptions of communication shape what systems are built and how their success is judged.
requirements: An explicit, articulated conception of communication, collaboration, and learning prior to system design
target_learners: Designers and researchers of computer-supported learning environments
target_learning_goals: Designing computer support for collaborative learning

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Three classroom chronotypes — adagio, andante, allegretto — characterize the co-constructed temporality of CSCL interaction
description: From the Ligorio and Ritella Bakhtinian analysis, the editorial presents temporality experienced by the classroom group as "a co-constructed encounter incorporating significant meaning and expression", not an objective, smooth succession of moments. Borrowing musical terminology, the authors "characterize phases of classroom interaction as proceeding with a tempo of adagio, andante, or allegretto"; the three chronotypes correspond to different modes of collaboration, coordinated with the simultaneously established sense of space, constructed by students' responses to each other under specific classroom and technology conditions.
requirements: Analysis of how interaction gradually unfolds during the period studied, rather than comparing initial to final states
constraints: Chronotypes are tied to the specific conditions of the classroom and its technology
target_learning_goals: Understanding how collaborative learning unfolds temporally in sequential interaction
examples: The editorial contrasts this with folk theories of learning that focus only on content changing from an initial to a final state.

citation: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2

description: The CDA (Chen et al., 2020) transforms uploaded lesson videos into synchronised transcripts and coloured bubbles sized by turn length, with statistics such as "Total Words" and word-share percentages per speaker, and a ranking function. In this study the research team used CDA to generate visualisations of teachers' lesson recordings that students viewed on iPads alongside clips during forum-based reflection. It had previously been applied in teacher professional learning and, in this study, supported young students' reflection on their own classroom talk.

Teachers select clips and devise reflection prompts for students
constraints: The researchers, not the teachers, generated the visualisations from the recordings

ICT/computational thinking subject knowledge

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Definition of classical PF studies: three shared characteristics distinguishing them from PF-similar studies
description: The article defines classical PF studies (e.g. Kapur 2010-2012; Loibl and Rummel 2014a, b; Westermann and Rummel 2012) as those that focus on STEM learning and "share the following three characteristics": (a) the problem-solving condition fulfilled the crucial design features of collaboratively inventing solution ideas to a complex problem and having erroneous student solutions compared and contrasted with the canonical solution; (b) effectiveness was tested with secondary school or undergraduate students; and (c) effectiveness was examined by comparing PF to an instruction-prior-to-problem-solving control condition. This yardstick frames the article's own two studies as a faithful transfer to a non-STEM domain.
requirements: The control condition must be an instruction prior to problem-solving approach so that only timing of instruction varies between conditions
Participants should be secondary school or undergraduate students
constraints: Classical PF studies as defined here focus on students' learning in a STEM domain (i.e., mathematics)

target_learning_goals: acquisition of conceptual knowledge in the targeted domain
examples: The two studies of this article emulate these characteristics: PF condition with collaborative invention and error-based instruction, 10th graders, comparison against a DI condition.

article_title: Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples
citation: Tim M. Steininger, Jörg Wittwer, Thamar Voss. (2022). Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09584-7
title: Use classification tasks rather than example generation in early phases of relational-category learning
description: The article recommends that when teaching concepts, learners should not generate their own examples in early phases of concept acquisition; instead, instruction should make heavier use of classification tasks in which learners reflect on which example belongs to which relational category. This rests on the finding that classifying was more effective and that generation produced overconfidence. Self-regulated learners are likewise advised to refrain from generating examples too early.

constraints: Recommended for early phases of concept acquisition; after initial understanding, generation might be more helpful for applying concepts to real-world contexts, which the article did not test
target_learners: student teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of relational categories such as types of knowledge in lesson planning
examples: In the experiment, the classifying group selected one of four knowledge types for each provided learning objective and received feedback, while the generating group wrote their own example learning objectives

citation: Meier, J., Hesse, P., Abele, S., Renkl, A., & Glogger-Frey, I. (2024). Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? title: Cognitive load theory (1998 conception) as the explanatory framework for prompt-direction and expertise effects in example-based learning
description: The article frames worked/modelling examples and self-explanation prompts through the 1998 conception of Cognitive Load Theory, which assumes limited working memory and three load types: germane, intrinsic, and extraneous. Prior knowledge reduces intrinsic load because "they already have cognitive schemas enabling them to combine multiple elements from the learning material and handle those as a single element in their working memory." The theory predicts anticipatory prompts raise both germane and intrinsic load, so only higher-prior-knowledge learners can manage them — the mechanism the study's moderation results were designed to test.

constraints: The authors deliberately use the 1998 conception rather than the 2019 revision to GCL concepts

citation: Melina Klepsch, Tina Seufert. (2020). Understanding instructional design effects by differentiated measurement of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load. Instructional Science (2020) 48:45–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09502-9

All items are rated on 7-point Likert-type scales. The article uses it across six studies to test whether intentional variations of one load type are reflected in the corresponding scale, finding prognostic validity to be good.

article_title: Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms
citation: Lin, YC., Liu, TC. & Kalyuga, S. (2022). Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms. Instructional Science, 50, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09600-w

description: The article develops instructional strategies grounded in cognitive load theory to address the transient information effect in instructional videos, where dynamic visualizations and spoken words disappear as they play. The strategies "provid[e] learners with explicit guidance in when and how to use pausing and timeline scrollbars while watching instructional videos," so that learners can re-expose and re-process transient material and integrate it with other representations. constraints: Effective learner control could be difficult to attain without sufficient instructional support
target_learning_goals: comprehension and recall of spoken and dynamic visual content in instructional videos
examples: Ninety undergraduates were randomly assigned to a strategy guidance group, a learner control group, or a continuous presentation group in a single-factor between-subjects experiment

article_title: How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach
citation: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3
title: Constructivist learning environment for argument structure training
description: A computerised training intervention conveying conceptual and procedural knowledge about the Toulmin model within a constructivist learning environment using Jonassen's (1999) cognitive modelling approach. It comprised a theoretical introduction with examples and learning goals, explanation prompts, two video tutorials modelling typical and atypical arguments with an expert model, twelve practice texts of varied argument types, and immediate feedback with a progress table. Participants could access theoretical information, tutorials, and notes at all stages.

clear learning goals matching the task

citation: Janssen, J., Kirschner, F., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Paas, F. (2010). Making the Black Box of Collaborative Learning Transparent: Combining Process-Oriented and Cognitive Load Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9131-x
title: Groups as information processing systems: a cognitive load account of collaborative learning balancing distribution advantage against transaction costs
description: The article advances a CLT-based account in which collaborating learners are viewed as information processing systems whose task information and associated load "can be divided across multiple collaborating WMs." This distribution advantage means collaborating individuals invest less cognitive effort than individuals learning alone, but interindividual communication and coordination impose transaction costs that can be germane (fostering shared understanding, argumentation, coordination) or extraneous (fostering errors, conflicts, unnecessary duplication). Whether collaboration beats individual learning depends on whether the distribution advantage compensates for extraneous transaction costs.

constraints: The article states CLT was developed for individual learning situations and that CLT-based collaborative studies did not monitor or analyze the specific transaction-cost processes

schema construction and automation
examples: The article interprets F. Kirschner et al.'s experiments on task complexity as demonstrating the trade-off between distribution advantage and transaction costs

Cueing behaviours direct attention before information enters working memory, reducing load; chunking behaviours encourage novices to construct, enrich and retrieve schemas after the bottleneck. title: The 1998 triarchic cognitive load theory model partitions working memory demands into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load
description: The review describes the 1998 CLT model (Sweller et al.) as partitioning working memory demands into three load types: intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, and germane load. Intrinsic load stems from element interactivity and varies with prior knowledge; extraneous load arises from design choices; germane load covers resources devoted to schema construction. The model assumes an additive relationship, so "intrinsic load and extraneous load must be low enough in order to leave sufficient cognitive resources for processes associated with germane load to occur".

constraints: Intrinsic load cannot be lowered by instructional design, only varied by learner prior knowledge

description: The review reports that Sweller et al. (2019) revised CLT in response to debates over germane load's definition and relevance, including factor-analytic arguments for a two-factor model. "The major change from the 1998 model is that Sweller et al. (2019) have removed germane load from the additive equation of total load, but rather a dimension now called 'germane processing.'" Consequently, increased germane load "is no longer believed to lead to cognitive overload and can thus no longer be assumed to be detrimental to learning performance".

description: The CL-REM is the article's proposed refinement of the Reciprocal Effects Model, drawing on the timescales continuum framework to formalize how self-concept and skills influence each other at different speeds. citation: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x
title: Classroom Carrying Capacity framework: an index of the maximum quality of support a classroom can provide students
description: Classroom Carrying Capacity adapts the biological concept of carrying capacity to classrooms, conceptualizing it as "an index of the maximum quality of support that is available to a student in the ecology of a classroom." Unlike traditional environmental models with binary thriving outcomes, CCC is a continuous metric reflecting the balance of resource factors (e.g., positive teacher-child relationships, effective instruction) outweighing limiting factors (e.g., problem behaviors, teacher burnout). title: Local dominance extension of the BFLPE: self-selected cliques as the most proximal reference group for adolescent ASC
description: This framework extends the big-fish-little-pond effect by adding the informal, self-selected clique as a reference group alongside the formal classroom. constraints: Findings are limited to mathematics ASC among sixth- and eighth-grade German secondary students in one school year; peer nominations were restricted to same-classroom peers, and only clique members were analyzed
target_learning_goals: development of academic self-concept in mathematics
examples: In the study, clique-average achievement negatively predicted ASC change while classroom-average achievement did not, supporting the clique as the more proximal reference group

article_title: External representation of argumentation in CSCL and the management of cognitive load
citation: Bruggen, J.M.; Kirschner, P.A.; Jochems, W. (2002). External representation of argumentation in CSCL and the management of cognitive load. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16871
title: Cognitive load theory as an analytical framework for CSCL: pinpointing situations of high cognitive load and mismatches between representations and tasks
description: The article positions cognitive load theory as a lens for analyzing CSCL environments where students share external representations of argumentation. CLT is said to "contribute to our understanding of CSCL by pinpointing situations in which high levels of cognitive load are generated" and to "help identify mismatches between representational schemes and execution of (sub)tasks." It thus functions as a diagnostic framework for locating load problems in collaborative settings rather than as a tested model.
requirements: CSCL environments with shared external representations of argumentation to which CLT analysis is applied
constraints: The article offers this as a reflection on research opportunities, not as an empirically validated account
target_learning_goals: argumentation and collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The authors relate CLT recommendations on integrating diagrammatic and textual information to discussion and chat facilities in CSCL
key_sources: Bruggen, J.M.; Kirschner, P.A.; Jochems, W. (2002). External representation of argumentation in CSCL and the management of cognitive load. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16871

article_title: The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school
citation: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e
title: Use classroom-level, evidence-based procedures such as the good behavior game and Daily Behavior Report Cards to prevent behavioral problems in elementary classrooms
description: The authors argue that, unlike individual case-based psychologically oriented support systems, only a few classroom-level support procedures have proven effective in school contexts. They name "the good behavior game", an interdependent group contingency procedure using playful elements to reduce classroom and behavioral disruptions, and "Daily Behavior Report Cards", in which the teacher works with the child to develop behaviors or goals for specific situations. Both are recommended as preventive measures within multi-tiered school-based support systems.
requirements: Whole-class implementation capacity (good behavior game) or teacher–child goal setting (Daily Behavior Report Cards)
constraints: The article cites effectiveness from prior reviews and meta-analyses (Flower et al., 2014; Pyle & Fabiano, 2017); this study did not test these procedures itself
target_learners: elementary school students, especially children with early behavioral problems
target_learning_goals: reducing classroom disruptions and externalizing problem behaviors; supporting adequate learning progress
examples: The authors state the good behavior game can be conducted with the entire class, and Daily Behavior Report Cards target reducing externalizing problem behaviors.
key_sources: Kulakow, S., Mahlau, K., & Kocaj, A. (2023). The longitudinal relationship between internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems with academic achievement in elementary school. https://osf.io/cyqak/?view_only=37eade9dd7c142e88fe9bef9451c125e

article_title: Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning
citation: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884
title: Cognitive load theory's cognitive architecture: limited working memory with partly independent visual and audio units interacting with unlimited long-term memory
description: The editorial presents the cognitive architecture on which cognitive load theory is based. As printed, it "is based on a cognitive architecture that consists of a limited working memory, with partly independent processing units for visual and audio information, which interacts with an unlimited long-term memory." This architecture grounds the special issue's instructional implications, framing why instruction must manage load across modality-specific channels and why long-term memory schemata offset working-memory limits.
requirements: Instructional designs derived from the theory must respect the limited capacity of working memory and its partly independent visual and audio processing units
target_learners: learners generally, across the domains covered in the special issue
target_learning_goals: optimising intellectual performance through load-managed instruction
examples: The editorial uses this architecture to introduce six articles on instructional techniques for managing cognitive load
key_sources: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884

article_title: Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning
citation: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884
title: Present information in ways that encourage learner activities that optimise intellectual performance
description: The editorial frames cognitive load theory as a source of presentation guidelines for instruction. It states that "Cognitive load theory (CLT) can provide guidelines to assist in the presentation of information in a manner that encourages learner activities that optimise intellectual performance." The principle directs designers to arrange information presentation so that learner activity is channeled productively rather than wasted on extraneous load, and the special issue articles instantiate this for worked examples, multimedia, and CSCL.
requirements: Designers need an analysis of which learner activities the presentation induces and how these relate to working-memory load
target_learners: learners generally, across the domains covered in the special issue
target_learning_goals: optimising intellectual performance through information presentation
examples: The special issue applies the principle to worked examples, example elaboration training, high element interactivity material, older learners, multimedia learning, and CSCL external representations

article_title: Class composition effects in achievement and interest and the role of the learning environment revisited: A conceptual replication and extension of Lavrijsen et al. (2022).
citation: Kopatz, M., Wagner, W., Neuendorf, C., Trautwein, U., Nagengast, B., and Bardach, L. (2025). Class Composition Effects in Achievement and Interest and the Role of the Learning Environment Revisited: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Lavrijsen et al. (2022). Preprint. https://osf.io/n5xur/?view_only=48daea427ab44c9abd13b21b1e2b42f6
title: Class composition effects framework
description: The article organizes its inquiry around composition effects, which "occur when individual student characteristics (e.g., individual academic achievement) are combined into a class-level composite score (e.g., mean academic achievement) and that score is related to individual-level outcomes (e.g., academic achievement) beyond student-level characteristic." The framework spans mean-level composition (achievement, interest) and within-class heterogeneity dimensions, tested at the classroom level with individual-level outcomes, and extended to motivational composition and learning-environment mediators. It guides the study's hypotheses about who benefits from which composition.
requirements: Class-level composites must be estimated beyond student-level characteristics (e.g., subtracting individual prior achievement) to isolate composition effects and avoid phantom effects.
constraints: The study focuses on classmates, since in German secondary schooling the class is the most proximal school-related developmental context.
target_learners: secondary school students in nonacademic-track classes in Germany
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics and German
subject-specific academic interest
examples: The study estimated class mean and heterogeneity effects on achievement and interest in mathematics and German classes using three-wave TRAIN data.

article_title: Methods and results of a class experiment in learning.
citation: Dearborn, W. F., and Brewer, J. M. (1918). Methods and Results of a Class Experiment in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. IX, No. 2. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/9/2/
title: Class experiment pattern: a practiced class and unpracticed control classes taking identical pre- and post-tests to study practice, transfer, and interference
description: The article demonstrates a class experiment in which one class practices a skill (translating English into a code) for twenty-two trials while control classes take the same five tests without intervening practice, twelve working days apart. Students plot their own learning curves, compute percentage gains, compare morning and evening performances, and write discussions of transfer and interference. The design lets a class illustrate individual differences, learning-curve characteristics, correlation, and facilitation or interference, with the article noting that "An unpracticed or control group is needed in order to test this question."
requirements: Test intervals should be the same in all groups; the article notes circumstances made this impossible in the present experiment, with intervals of sixteen, nine, and nineteen calendar days.
constraints: Materials must be tasks in which the student is not already practiced and in which improvement is possible within a relatively short practice; the article calls the tasks used artificial and recommends more useful ones.
target_learning_goals: understanding of practice effects, transfer, interference, and experimental method
examples: The practiced class in educational psychology was practiced twenty-two times in the use of a code between the two administrations of the five tests, while classes in teaching and school administration took the tests without intervening practice.
key_sources: Dearborn, W. F., and Brewer, J. M. (1918). Methods and Results of a Class Experiment in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. IX, No. 2. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/9/2/

article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: Analyze student evaluations of secondary teaching at the class-mean level, aligned with parallel teacher reports for the same class
description: The article argues that because inferences concern the shared classroom experience and the teacher's practice, student ratings should be aggregated to class means rather than analyzed at the student level: "we evaluate student ratings at the class-mean level and align them with parallel teacher reports for the same class." Student-level analyses confound within- and between-class variance and underreport reliability at the teacher/class level, a critique the article traces to prior secondary-school SET research.
requirements: Ratings collected in intact classrooms with each student evaluating a single identified class
Class records linked to the corresponding teacher's parallel self-rating via class identifiers
constraints: Classes with fewer than five students were excluded to reduce unreliability in small aggregates
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of classroom-level teaching effectiveness for formative feedback
examples: In the validation analyses, student ratings were aggregated to 1,013 class-mean responses aligned with 549 teacher self-evaluations

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of chemistry.
citation: Ellwood B. Spear. (1915). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Chemistry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Connect laboratory experiments illustrating related phenomena so pupils more readily correlate ideas.
description: The article recommends choosing laboratory experiments that are correlated with one another rather than isolated illustrations of single points. It argues that "the pupil's chances of realizing the relation between synthesis and metathesis would be greatly enhanced by having the experiments illustrating the two phenomena closely connected," yet notes this device is seldom used in laboratory manuals. The copper-sulphur sequence (combination then treatment with nitric acid) is given as a worked example.
requirements: Experiments must be selected so that successive ones illustrate related chemical phenomena, such as synthesis and metathesis, using shared materials.
constraints: The article presents this as a reasoned expectation, stating it holds "until we have evidence to the contrary," and notes the device is seldom made use of in existing laboratory manuals.
target_learning_goals: correlation of ideas
connecting chemical facts and theory
examples: Heating copper and sulphur to show combination, then treating the copper sulphide with nitric acid to show metathesis, followed by seven linked experiments extending from copper nitrate through deliquescence, diffusion, and hydrates.

article_title: Communications and discussions: Notes on the recall of nonsense syllables.
citation: Whipple, G. M. (1917). Notes on the recall of nonsense syllables. Cornell University. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Use documented incidental-retention incidents as classroom illustrations of the nature of retention and recall in educational psychology teaching
description: The author proposes that observations like the nonsense-syllable case have value for teaching educational psychology, because they give students a verifiable, classmate-sourced instance of long-term retention. He notes stock anecdotes such as the Coleridge servant-girl story are striking but lack the certainty of an instance "drawn from the experience of classmates". Such illustrations can also address the familiar student query of whether anything is absolutely forgotten.
requirements: The original learning experience must be a matter of record so that recall can be verified against it
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of retention and recall
evaluating the reliability of memory for long-forgotten incidents
examples: The author placed ten nonsense syllables on the blackboard for memorization during a class discussion, later tested former students' recall, and used the records as teaching illustrations

article_title: The truth sandwich format does not enhance the correction of misinformation.
citation: Swire-Thompson, Briony, Butler, Lucy, & Rapp, David N. (2025). The truth sandwich format does not enhance the correction of misinformation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(6), 851–862. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000961
title: Prioritize clear, coherent correction content over the ordering format of corrective information
description: This principle holds that what matters in a misinformation correction is the quality and completeness of the corrective content, not the order of its components. In two experiments, fact-first and misinformation-first corrections were equally effective, leading the authors to conclude that "Making corrections clear and coherent is likely far more important than ensuring they buttress or bookend misinformation in any particular way." Communicators should therefore invest effort in correction clarity rather than in elaborate formats.
requirements: Corrections must contain the necessary components — the misinformation identified as false plus factual corrective information — which the article states are "highly useful for fostering belief change, irrespective of their format".
constraints: Evidence comes from short format, health-based misinformation; the authors note future research should replicate the findings with other misinformation content, correction types, or contexts.
target_learners: US adults encountering health misinformation (Prolific samples over age 18)
target_learning_goals: Reduce belief in false claims
Reduce reliance on misinformation when reasoning
examples: Participants received corrections in which the same three sections were simply reordered into truth sandwich or bottom-loaded refutation formats, counterbalanced in a Latin Square design across participants.

article_title: Native learning ability and not age determines the effects of brain stimulation
citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y
title: Classifier-based learner stratification model predicting likelihood to benefit from atDCS from baseline task performance
description: A machine-learning framework that labels individuals as "optimal" or "suboptimal" learners of a finger-tapping task from age and baseline speed and accuracy, then projects the distance to the separating hyperplane onto a sigmoid function to estimate each person's likelihood of benefiting from stimulation. The article reports "achieving a prediction accuracy of 97% (i.e., F1 score)" on training data, and each class is split into high and low tiers by median split. It embodies the hypothesis that optimal acquisition relies on prioritizing accuracy improvement early in training.
requirements: Training data from unstimulated or placebo-stimulated participants of a prior dataset, excluding verum groups so no verum data trains the model
Baseline block and first training block measurements of speed and accuracy plus age as features
constraints: The 97% F1 score only indicates the separability of the training features, since no validation set was held aside
The model estimates the native state of the neural system indirectly, depending on relative performance between the baseline block and the first training block
target_learners: healthy young, middle-aged, and older adults learning a sequential motor task
target_learning_goals: acquisition of sequential motor skills (finger-tapping)
examples: A 2nd-degree polynomial expansion and 10-fold cross-validation selected a support-vector classifier as the best model
