article_title: High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype
citation: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8
title: Schedule skill practice closely after exercise cessation to exploit the exercise priming window
description: The article operationalised exercise priming by timing "Motor skill training on the SVIPT 62 was timed to commence 10-minutes after exercise, in line with previous studies reporting a maximal priming effect when there is a close temporal coupling between exercise and learning". It also cites evidence that facilitative physiological effects are prominent 15–30 minutes after HIIT and that closer coupling yields greater benefit. Skill learning was detected in the HIIT group from about 16.5 minutes after exercise cessation.
requirements: Practice must follow exercise within the priming window; this study used a 10-minute delay between exercise cessation and task commencement.
constraints: The observed facilitation was for a task with a protracted learning trajectory (SVIPT); prior work with a rapidly plateauing task (SRTT) practised on average 35 minutes post HIIT and found no benefit, so timing and task demands jointly matter.
target_learners: Healthy young adults in motor skill training
target_learning_goals: Enhancing acquisition of novel motor skills
examples: Participants completed a 20-minute HIIT bout followed by a 1–2-minute cool down, with SVIPT practice beginning 10 minutes after exercise.
key_sources: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8

article_title: Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests
citation: Britt Hadar, Maayan Katzir, Sephi Pumpian, Tzur Karelitz and Nira Liberman. (2023). Psychological proximity improves reasoning in academic aptitude tests. npj Science of Learning 8:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00158-x
title: Construal level theory account of opposing distance/proximity predictions for reasoning
description: The article organizes its hypotheses with construal level theory (CLT), which "proposes that objects that are distal in time, space, or social perspective or are uncertain (i.e., distant on the dimension of hypotheticality), are mentally represented (i.e., construed) on a higher level of abstraction". It uses CLT to derive two opposing predictions: distance fosters abstraction that filters irrelevant details and groups information, reducing working-memory load, while proximity yields concrete, vivid, detailed representations that are processed with more attention, each plausibly aiding reasoning. The three studies test these competing accounts empirically.
requirements: Reasoning problems whose extraneous content (objects, people, times, places) can be rewritten as psychologically proximal or distal while retaining logical structure
constraints: Prior knowledge activated by proximity or distance is superfluous to solving the problems correctly, by the article's design
target_learners: Examinees solving verbal reasoning problems on aptitude assessments
target_learning_goals: Correct solution of verbal reasoning problems requiring accurate representation of parameters and mapping onto a logical structure
examples: Studies 1–3 contrasted proximal versions (objects and places in participants' culture, ingroup members, recent past) against distal versions (distant cultures, unfamiliar groups, distant past).

article_title: Effects of videos with whole-body movements on young children’s geography learning
citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Integration of cognitive load theory and embodied cognition for digital movement-based learning
description: The article combines an evolutionary upgrade of cognitive load theory with embodied cognition to design and interpret digital movement-based learning. Physical actions are treated as a form of biologically primary knowledge serving as "cognitive offloading" mechanisms that may reduce working memory burden, while sensorimotor, multimodal representations are held to convey object properties and support memory encoding. In the study, movements also "fulfilled an analogous role of 'segmentation'", consolidating transient video information. The authors state that no measures were included to test the proposed mechanisms, so the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative.
requirements: Movements should be relevant to and temporally connected with the goal-directed learning task; complementary information presented across modalities without repetition
constraints: No cognitive load measures were included, so whether cognitive load was induced or alleviated in the embodied group cannot be inferred; overly cognitive or coordinatively demanding movements can impede learning
target_learners: Young children learning via digital environments
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition in STEM domains such as geography through digitally supported embodied activity
examples: The game-based geography task was designed on cognitive load theory, embodied and experiential learning principles, with movements segmenting transient spoken text and animations
key_sources: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8

article_title: Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms
citation: Xiaomeng Xu, Dan Zhang & Yu Zhang. (2026). Student teacher inter brain coupling forecast cross semester academic fluctuation in real world classrooms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00421-x
title: Longitudinal wearable-EEG hyperscanning dataset from 393 authentic classroom sessions
description: A longitudinal observational dataset of classroom inter-brain coupling: "a total of 4,175 longitudinal EEG recordings were collected from 107 junior and senior students across 393 regular Chinese and math classes" over three semesters (six waves), using dual-channel dry-electrode headbands at Fp1/Fp2 sampled at 250 Hz. Outcomes are rank-based normalized half-semester exam scores. The dataset supports student-teacher, student-class and student-excellence coupling analyses with lag-0 validated by a bootstrapped mismatched-pairing baseline.
requirements: Student-teacher pairs required at least six valid matched epochs per session, and students with valid sessions below 20% within a wave were omitted
constraints: Devices were limited to two channels to minimize disruption; the recorded lessons reflect routine, non-intervention instruction
target_learners: junior and senior secondary school students in Beijing, China
target_learning_goals: Chinese and math academic achievement
examples: Lag coupling analysis compared matched TI against 148,593 non-matched pairings, with TI reliably higher only at lag 0 (t = 2.247, p = 0.024) and lag +1

article_title: Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions
citation: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z
title: Classical twin design partitions trait variance into additive genetic, shared environmental, and non-shared environmental influences
description: The classical twin design exploits that "twins share either all (identical or monozygotic twins) or half (non-identical or dizygotic twins) of their genes". Comparing monozygotic and dizygotic twin correlations partitions variance into additive genetic influences (A/heritability), shared environmental influences (C), and non-shared environmental influences (E). Heritability is indicated when the monozygotic correlation exceeds the dizygotic correlation; shared environment is estimated by subtracting heritability from the monozygotic correlation, and non-shared environment by subtracting the monozygotic correlation from one.
requirements: Samples of related individuals differing in genetic relatedness (monozygotic vs dizygotic twins) or environmental exposure (monozygotic twins reared apart)
constraints: Classical twin studies are limited for disentangling genetic confounds because both twin types commonly share their rearing environment, so monozygotic and dizygotic resemblance cannot be compared for shared environmental measures like home library or household income
target_learners: children and adolescents in behavioral-genetics twin research
target_learning_goals: estimating sources of individual differences in traits such as reading ability and school achievement
examples: In Grade-2 word-reading fluency data from van Bergen et al., monozygotic and dizygotic twin correlations were 0.84 and 0.46, yielding Falconer-formula estimates A = 0.76, C = 0.08, E = 0.16
key_sources: Hart, S. A., Little, C. & van Bergen, E. (2021). Nurture might be nature: cautionary tales and proposed solutions. npj Science of Learning 6:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00079-z

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: Educational technologies should be thoroughly tested before classroom availability, on the medical clinical-trials model
description: Drawing on a Council of Europe project, the author argues that because society insists medical interventions are thoroughly tested before wide availability due to safety and efficacy implications for the human body, 'we should insist on educational technologies being thoroughly tested before being made available in classrooms (because of their safety and efficacy implications for the developing human mind)'. The project also works toward a recommendation that teaching about AI include both human and technological dimensions.
requirements: A legal instrument to govern the application of AI in educational settings is being developed to operationalise this
constraints: The work is situated in a Council of Europe project addressing teaching with AI and teaching about AI
target_learning_goals: Ensuring safety and efficacy of AI tools used in education
examples: The Council of Europe project is drawing on the medical model of clinical trials for a legal instrument governing AI in education
key_sources: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3

article_title: Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition
citation: Adelson de Araujo, Pantelis M. Papadopoulos, Susan McKenney, Ton de Jong. (2025). Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00469-7
title: Clair, a CCA with six APT-based talk moves triggered via dialogue variables and a fuzzy expert system
description: Clair is a Collaborative Conversational Agent integrated into the Go-Lab chat tool that guides student-student dialogue using APT principles. It uses six talk moves (Checking-in, Peer questioning, Reorienting, Peer coordination, What-if, Press for reasoning), two of which are proactive rather than reactive. Talk moves are triggered from fifteen automatic 'dialogue variables' based on ConSent classifiers built on the multilingual Universal Sentence Encoder, interpreted by "a fuzzy expert system designed to interpret whether a talk move could be used" with fuzzy sets (high, medium, low) and one inference rule per talk move.
requirements: Student dyads must use the chat tool for collaboration so interventions can reach the intended audience; classifiers depend on the pre-trained mUSE encoder
constraints: Dyads with one or zero Clair interventions were excluded from analysis; some dyads excessively focused on asking questions to Clair rather than engaging their peer
target_learners: secondary school students (14-16-year-old, HAVO/VWO) in dyads
target_learning_goals: dialogue productivity via APT goals
collaborative inquiry learning about enzymes and digestion
examples: The What-if talk move poses hypothetical variations of nine standard statements from the orientation phase, e.g., what would happen if the enzyme in saliva was exposed to very high temperatures

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education

description: The thesis outlines cognitive load theory (CLT) and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML) as purely cognitive frameworks. description: The article proposes three non-exclusive hypotheses to explain its counterintuitive note-production findings. title: Classroom structure as a multifaceted set of teacher practices distinct from control, with chaos as its logical opposite
description: The article defines classroom structure as "teachers’ attempts to create an organized and predictable environment that helps students effectively achieve desired outcomes", drawing on self-determination theory, instructional quality, and classroom management literatures that use largely synonymous definitions under different labels. Structure comprises practices such as communicating clear expectations, rules, and goals; framing activity with directions, routines, or schedules; organizing space and materials; monitoring progress; and giving encouragement and feedback about accomplishing desired outcomes. The construct is explicitly distinguished from control: whereas control constrains students to act in teacher-determined ways, structure provides competence-relevant information that supports self-regulation, and its logical opposite is chaos, in which teachers are confusing, contradictory, or disorganized.
requirements: Structure must be implemented as practices providing clarity of information and ongoing guidance rather than demands and sanctions that pressure students to act in teacher-determined ways
constraints: The benefits of structure can be constrained when teachers compliment structure with controlling practices or apply structure in a controlling manner

title: Taxonomy of classroom-based physical activity forms and academic-related outcome categories
description: The review organises classroom-based physical activity into three forms — active breaks, curriculum-focussed active breaks, and physically active lessons — defined as "physical activity carried out during regular class time", distinct from recess or lunch breaks. cognitive function
academic achievement
examples: The review categorised the 39 included studies as 19 active break, 7 curriculum-focussed active break, and 13 physically active lesson interventions, and conducted separate meta-analyses per outcome category

description: The article recommends structuring an eduXR review ecosystem "as a closed loop managed by feedback and incentive structures to ensure stability and productivity". article_title: Effectiveness of Constructivist Approach on Academic Achievement in Science at Secondary Level
citation: Samaresh Adak. (2017). Effectiveness of constructivist approach on academic achievement in science at secondary level. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3298

description: The study's measuring tools comprised Raven's Progressive Matrices, used for grouping students by intelligence, and a teacher-made achievement test based on constructivist (7E-model) principles covering the Class IX Textbook of the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education. The test was administered as pre-test and post-test to both groups, and its scores supplied the means, gain scores, t-tests and ANOVA reported in the findings.

constraints: A teacher-made instrument limited to two physical science lessons; other units were not covered
target_learning_goals: measuring achievement in physical science before and after instruction
examples: Pre-test and post-test scores from this test produced the reported means, gain scores, t-tests and ANOVA

article_title: Effects of Cloze Instructional Approach on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Igbo Language Reading Comprehension
citation: Nneka Justina Eze. (2015). Effects of Cloze Instructional Approach on Senior Secondary School Students' Achievement in Igbo Language Reading Comprehension. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. http://www.iiste.org
title: Cloze procedure grounded in Gestalt closure and total language context
description: The article grounds the cloze instructional approach in the Gestalt theory of CLOSURE founded by Max Wertheimer, under which human beings tend to perceive unfinished or incomplete figures as complete, filling in gaps in broken patterns with their mental framework, with patterns understood as linguistic in nature. Wilson Taylor, credited with designing the cloze test in 1953, viewed a cloze unit as any single occurrence of a successful attempt to reproduce accurately a part deleted from a message by deciding from the context that remains what the missing part should be. Taylor's theoretical consideration came from the concept of total language context, anchored on the finding that language behaviours are dependent on total context. The article uses this account to explain why filling gaps in a passage depends on learners' ability to make genuine analysis of basic concepts and form a conceptual whole that determines a passage's comprehensibility.
requirements: Learners must be able to make genuine analysis of basic concepts in the passage so as to form a conceptual whole
constraints: Its efficacy in Igbo language had not been empirically validated before this study
target_learners: Senior secondary school students learning Igbo language
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of Igbo language text
examples: The treatment group was taught Igbo language using the cloze instructional approach, with both fixed and variable ratio cloze utilized

article_title: Structuring Cooperative Learning in Teaching English Pronunciation
citation: Hsuan-Yu Chen (Jack) & Jaya S. Goswami. (2011). Structuring Cooperative Learning in Teaching English Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 4(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n3p26
title: Cooperative learning model built on five essential elements
description: The article adopts the Johnson & Johnson (1989) cooperative learning model, in which "The cooperative learning (CL) model incorporates five essential elements: positive interdependence; individual accountability; face-to-face promotive interaction; social skills; and group processing." These elements must be carefully structured into cooperative groups so that additive learning outcomes can be anticipated. The study operationalized them through jigsaw tasks, Bingo games, team names, and weekly group processing sessions.
requirements: The five elements need to be carefully structured into cooperative learning groups for the additive learning outcome to be anticipated
constraints: In ELL classrooms, attention must be paid to incubation time for CL elements and social and cultural factors
target_learners: English language learners in ESL pronunciation classes
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation of difficult target consonants
communication and academic achievement through supportive peer interaction
examples: The jigsaw activity assigned each member a different target-sound pair (b/v, sh/ch, s/z) to master and teach back to the home group, incorporating individual accountability, positive interdependence, social skills, face-to-face interaction, and group processing

article_title: The Impact of Using "Pixton" for Teaching Grammar and Vocabulary in the EFL Ecuadorian Context
citation: Cabrera, P., Castillo, L., González, P., Quiñónez, A., & Ochoa, C. (2018). The impact of using Pixton for teaching grammar and vocabulary in the EFL Ecuadorian context. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 53-76. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Give students clear instructions when using Pixton comic-strip activities with young learners
description: The article's conclusions state that "Clear instructions, as an essential part of the teachers' methodology when using activities with Pixton, are indispensable for successful vocabulary and grammar learning when teaching young students." This principle treats instruction clarity as a precondition for comic-strip-based activities to support grammar and vocabulary learning. It is grounded in the study's questionnaire and observation findings that teachers' instructions were perceived as clear and that teachers reported no difficulty providing clear explanations.
requirements: Teachers must provide clear instructions when setting Pixton-based activities
constraints: The principle is stated for young students in the study's EFL junior-high context
target_learning_goals: EFL grammar knowledge
EFL vocabulary knowledge
examples: In the study, 41.51% of students believed their teachers' instructions were very clear when using comic strips and 38.99% perceived them as clear

article_title: The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students' Classroom Engagement in Teaching English
citation: Ayçiçek, B., & Yanpar Yelken, T. (2018). The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students’ Classroom Engagement in Teaching English. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 385-398. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11226a
title: Classroom Engagement Inventory (Turkish adaptation, 23 items, five sub-factors)
description: The study's outcome instrument is the "Classroom Engagement Inventory" developed by Wang, Bergin and Bergin (2014) and adapted to Turkish by Sever (2014). After adaptation it retained 23 Likert-type items (20 positive, 3 negative) scored on a 5-point scale from "always" to "never", covering five sub-factors: "Cognitive Engagement", "Affective Engagement", "Behavioural Engagement -Compliance", "Behavioral Engagement - Effortful Classroom Participation", and "Disengagement". Recalculated reliability was Cronbach alpha = .93, and confirmatory factor analysis was rerun because the scale was originally developed for high school students but applied to secondary school students (RMSEA=0.056; AGFI=0.955; RMR=0.066; GFI=0.951).
requirements: Administered before and after the four-week application to both groups; students assumed to reflect their real opinions
constraints: Originally developed for high school students, so confirmatory factor analysis was carried out again for secondary school use
target_learning_goals: classroom engagement in English courses (affective, behavioural and cognitive engagement, and disengagement)
examples: Given to the experimental and control groups before and after the four-week flipped classroom experiment

title: CLIL applications planned through the 4Cs following the Coyle, Hood and Marsh guide
description: This pattern structures content-subject lessons as CLIL applications attending to the 4Cs: Content (subject topics), Communication (the four language skills), Cognition (Bloom's LOTS and HOTS) and Culture (the socio-cultural context as a thread through each application). The teachers "developed a total of 17 applications in which the 4Cs are taken into account according to CLIL", planned following the guide established by Coyle, Hood and Marsh (2010): define content, link it to communication, explore cognitive abilities, and establish culture contextually.
requirements: Planning guided by an expert CLIL teacher through LOCIT accompaniment
Selection of subjects and topics coherent with the students' English level
constraints: Applications were designed for first-semester Nursing program subjects at English level A1.1 of the CEFR
target_learners: First-level (A1.1) English students in higher education Nursing programs
target_learning_goals: English communicative competence
Cognitive skills applied through a foreign language
examples: Six teachers of the seven first-semester Nursing subjects designed lesson plans and worksheets guided by an expert teacher through LOCIT, with greater emphasis on Writing and Reading skills and on the LOTS Understanding and Applying.

description: Clustering is an idea-generation technique the article describes as helping writers "arrange, generate and develop the writers' ideas in order to product a good writing." article_title: Improving Universal Classroom Practices through Teacher Formative Assessment and Coaching
citation: Christopher M. Dudek, MEd, Linda A. Reddy, PhD, Adam Lekwa, PhD, Anh N. Hua, PhD, and Gregory A. Fabiano, PhD. (2019). Improving Universal Classroom Practices Through Teacher Formative Assessment and Coaching. Assessment for Effective Intervention. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508418772919
title: Classroom Strategies Coaching (CSC) Model
description: The CSC Model is a brief, data-driven instructional coaching approach grounded in behavioral consultation frameworks and active learning techniques from systems and social learning theories. Teachers are "active collaborators and decision makers" while coaches conduct classroom observations, model strategies, provide practice opportunities, and deliver data-informed feedback. It proceeds in four phases: identifying practice needs and goals from CSAS baseline data, developing and implementing plans for a first set of targeted strategies, defining and modeling a second set, and sustaining improvements through preplanning and recall strategies. It targets both instructional and behavior management strategies as universal practices.
requirements: Coaches trained on a manualized approach with session procedural checklists and weekly supervision
Ongoing classroom observations between coaching sessions using the CSAS to provide data-informed feedback
constraints: The current study's pre–post design without a comparison group precludes firm causal conclusions
Long-term effects on teacher practices were not assessed
target_learning_goals: evidence-based instructional strategies
classroom behavior management strategies
examples: Coaches reviewed baseline CSAS data with teachers and collaboratively selected two to four practice goals from the eight strategy counts
Four 30-minute weekly coaching sessions over approximately 4 weeks, with goal-presentation order counterbalanced across Sessions 2 and 3

citation: Tagor Pangaribuan & Sondang Manik. (2018). The Effect of Buzz Group Technique and Clustering Technique in Teaching Writing at the First Class of SMA HKBP I Tarutung. English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p164
title: Clustering technique as a visual pre-writing brainstorming method
description: The article defines clustering as a pre-writing brainstorming technique, citing Hoshima and Hogue (1991), in which "the write make s a circle in the centre of the paper then draws the lines while the writer gets the ideas in mind." Also called mapping, webbing, or diagramming, it is classified as a chaotic process that depends on subconscious knowledge and frees the writer from structural rules. The article states "there is no exact rule like which is right and which is wrong in clustering" and that it is "more helpful for the writer who thinks visually in getting ideas before the actually write the first draft of the writing."
requirements: The writer must have narrowed to a specific topic before clustering begins, as the article states it is used "after the writer focuses or norrows to the specifi c topic."
constraints: The article classifies clustering as a chaotic rather than structured process, meaning it "depends on the subconcius knowledge that people have."
target_learners: first-year senior high school students (Class X)
target_learning_goals: generating and visually connecting ideas in pre-writing for descriptive text composition
examples: The article divided Class X students into an experimental group using clustering in pre-writing activities across eight meetings before a descriptive text post-test.

citation: Karimi, P., Lotfi, A. R., & Biria, R. (2019). Enhancing Pilot’s Aviation English Learning, Attitude and Motivation through the Application of Content and Language Integrated Learning. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 751-766. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Use CLIL to teach specialized occupational English content to enhance learning, attitude, and motivation
description: The article recommends Content and Language Integrated Learning for teaching English for Occupational Purposes, in which subject content serves as the medium for learning language items. In the study, the experimental group received instruction through CLIL with a subject matter teacher for the first 45 minutes and an EFL teacher for the second 45 minutes, while the control group was taught by a traditional approach with only a subject matter teacher. The findings suggest important implications for course designers and teachers working in EOP.

constraints: The article notes the limitation of paucity of the students, since the ICAO rule for the number of students in an aviation class is between 16 and 20.

content knowledge of aviation subject matter
positive attitudes and motivation toward English learning
examples: Forty male pilots at Mahan Airlines headquarters training center studied the aircraft weight and balance course through CLIL or a traditional approach in a pretest-posttest experimental design.

article_title: Effectiveness of Gamification of Web-Based Learning in Improving Academic Achievement and Creative Thinking among Primary School Students
citation: Aljraiwi, S. (2019). Effectiveness of Gamification of Web-Based Learning in Improving Academic Achievement and Creative Thinking Among Primary School Students. International Journal of Education and Practice, 7(3), 242-257. https://doi.org/10.18488/journal.61.2019.73.242.257
title: ClassDojo-based gamified web-based learning environment for primary English
description: The author designed a learning environment for the "My Language" English course built on the ClassDojo platform, which Williamson (2017) defines as "a commercial platform for tracking students’ behavior data in classrooms and a social media network for connecting teachers, students and parents." Each lesson is a level; learners earn points on formative assessment and repeat a level if points fall below a set threshold. Points are tied to a 60-second timer, and competitive and collaborative badges reward individual and team performance.
requirements: Teachers run a formative assessment at the end of each lesson-level to award points and decide whether the learner repeats the level or advances
constraints: The leaderboard "may be strongly disappointing when a learner observes how far they are behind"
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in English
Creative thinking skills (fluency, flexibility, originality)
examples: Points were linked to answer speed: a learner answering in 30 seconds received 30 extra points for the correct answer

article_title: Using Clickers to Enhance Student Learning in Mathematics
citation: Ye Wang, Chia-Jung Chung & Lihua Yang. (2014). Using Clickers to Enhance Student Learning in Mathematics. International Education Studies, 7(10). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n10p1
title: Clickers (Student Response System) handheld transmitters with instant feedback and anonymous responding
description: Clickers are "small transmitters about the size of a television remote control" used within a Student Response System, transmitting answers by infrared or radio frequency. Students respond anonymously and the cumulative class view appears on a public screen; teachers collect results instantly, can download and store them digitally, review individual scores, and re-teach concepts where students struggle. constraints: Students cannot enter answers containing fractions, rational numbers, or special mathematics symbols such as % and π; some students were stressed by unfamiliar special keys.
target_learners: high school Geometry students, including ELL and Special Education students
target_learning_goals: formative assessment, instant feedback, anonymous participation, mathematics learning
examples: Students picked up clickers on entering the classroom and submitted warm-up, homework quiz, class work, and summative assessment answers; contrast-group students used white boards, paper, and scantrons.

article_title: Longitudinal Impacts of the Children's Literacy Initiative Professional Development, Coaching, and Model Classroom Intervention on Early Literacy Achievement

title: Establish classroom norms and protocols that guide team behaviour before co-operative learning
description: The article states "It is important, however, to establish classroom norms and protocols that guide students to" contribute, stay on task, help each other, encourage each other, share and solve problems. Norms are presented as a precondition for co-operative teams to function, preventing the same students from always performing the same tasks. The study's team activities were run within such an expectation structure.

citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Pas, E. T., Bottiani, J. H., Debnam, K. J., Reinke, W. M., Herman, K. C., & Rosenberg, M. S. (2018). title: Classroom Check-Up (CCU) coaching adapted for culturally responsive practices
description: The Classroom Check-Up is a data-based decision-making coaching model adapted for Double Check, in which "the coach and teacher go through five clear steps": rapport-building interview, data collection via the Classroom Ecology Checklist and three classroom observations, feedback on strengths and weaknesses, collaborative goal setting, and implementation with progress monitoring and fading support. culturally responsive practices
reduced exclusionary discipline referrals

article_title: A Comparative Study of Testing Grammar Knowledge of Iranian Students between Cloze and Multiple-Choice Tests
citation: Minoo Alemi & Apama Miraghaee. (2011). A Comparative Study of Testing Grammar Knowledge of Iranian Students between Cloze and Multiple-Choice Tests. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 1, No. 3, July - September 2011. https://www.i-manager.com
title: Cloze tests as integrative, pragmatic measures drawing on linguistic, textual and world knowledge
description: The article presents the cloze test as an integrative testing procedure rooted in holistic teaching approaches, requiring students to possess language components simultaneously. It reports the view that "three types of knowledge are required in order to perform successfully on a cloze test: linguistic knowledge, textual knowledge, and knowledge of the world", and cites Oller's argument that cloze tests satisfy pragmatic naturalness by requiring learners to process language under normal contextual and discourse-level constraints, which the article says generates strong validity coefficients.
requirements: Careful selection and preparation of alternative cloze tests at appropriate levels of reading difficulty, as the article states recent studies require
constraints: The article's own experiment found cloze testing did not develop grammar knowledge more than multiple-choice testing
target_learning_goals: grammar knowledge
general language proficiency
examples: The study used variable-ratio cloze passages with 25 blanks drawn from the students' reading book, with readability estimated in advance through Fog's formula

article_title: Infusing Cooperative Learning into an EFL Classroom
citation: Luu Trong Tuan. (2010). Infusing Cooperative Learning into An EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching. https://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Cooperative Learning as an environment resting on four elements: positive interdependence, individual accountability, quality of group interaction, and social skills instruction
description: The article defines Cooperative Learning via Johnson & Johnson as "the instructional use of small groups so that students work together to maximize their own and each other's learning", and stresses it "is not simply putting students together in groups". Teachers must guarantee four elements: positive interdependence (avoiding "hitchhiking"), individual accountability, quality of face-to-face group interaction in small groups, and explicit teaching of group-related and task-related social skills. The study operationalized these elements in its lesson designs.
requirements: Teachers must guarantee that the four elements transpire rather than merely assigning group tasks
Social skills require explicit instruction on communication, leadership, trust and conflict resolution
constraints: Without positive interdependence, learners fall into hitchhiking or being off task (Cohen, 1994)
target_learning_goals: EFL reading proficiency
cooperative interaction and social skills
examples: The first lesson used a video, a word game for grouping, and a jigsaw reading on doodles to establish the elements

article_title: Infusing Cooperative Learning into an EFL Classroom
citation: Luu Trong Tuan. (2010). Infusing Cooperative Learning into An EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching. https://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Introduce Cooperative Learning gradually, layer after layer, with teacher lecture as a transitional phase, because rushing produces learner resistance
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that Cooperative Learning be introduced patiently: learner resistance in the first weeks "displays teachers' rush", and implementation "should be structured layer after layer, much like peeling an onion, until the heart is reached" (Johnson et al., 1993). Smith and Waller's Cooperative Learning Lecture is recommended as a transitional phase from lecturing to Cooperative Learning, and students' requests for some lecture were accommodated.
requirements: Students need sufficient time to learn the abilities the approach demands (Stahl, 1992)
Teachers should invite students' inner thoughts on the new approach in spoken or written form
constraints: Learner resistance in the first few weeks occurred in this study when activities were introduced quickly
target_learners: first-year EFL university students accustomed to teacher-centered instruction
target_learning_goals: transition from teacher dependence to learner interdependence
examples: The researcher slowed down after the second lesson, gathered student feedback at break time, and used phone calls, e-mails and handouts to keep absent students connected to their groups

article_title: The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency
citation: Hassan Alrayah. (2018). The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p21
title: Classical learning theory's four dimensions as applied to Cooperative Learning
description: The article names Classical Learning Theory as the second grounding theory and says it "encompasses four dimensions: 1) Reinforcement 2) Correction opportunity 3) Practice opportunity 4) Transference." It applies each to cooperative classrooms: cooperative learning increases the immediacy and desirability of rewards; correction from classmates is "immediate, frequent, more equal, and supportive"; it minimizes teacher talking time and maximizes students' talking time; and because cooperative teams are social interaction positions, the acquisition situation resembles later performance situations, so cooperative learning "decreases the transference gap."
requirements: For reinforcement to work as described, the article argues for changing from delayed reinforcement to frequent reinforcement and from a smoothly desirable reward to a highly desirable reward.
constraints: The transference argument assumes the cooperative team situation resembles the situations in which students later implement the skills they have learnt.
target_learning_goals: Oral fluency of speaking through practice, feedback and transfer
examples: The article contrasts the traditional classroom, where students sit in rows and work alone and teacher talking time is maximized, with cooperative teams where students take turns contributing orally and in writing.

article_title: Student Academic Performance Outcomes of a Classroom Physical Activity Intervention: A Pilot Study
citation: Heather Erwin, Alicia Fedewa, Soyeon Ahn. (2012). Student Academic Performance Outcomes of a Classroom Physical Activity Intervention: A Pilot Study. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 4(3), 473-487. https://www.iejee.com
title: Classroom-based PA break intervention with teacher training and activity resources
description: A curricular intervention in which "The classroom teacher of the intervention group led PA breaks for 20+ minutes per day", each break relating to the math and reading content currently being taught. The teacher received a 30-minute classroom PA training from an expert covering PA definition, importance, and management, and was provided activity break cards and web resources. Control students continued traditional in-seat learning with equal PE and recess time.
requirements: Teacher training in classroom PA and instructional means for presenting activity breaks
Activity break cards and web resources for classroom physical activities
constraints: Compared against traditional in-seat instruction by homeroom class in a quasi-experimental design; both groups had identical PE (two 30-minute classes weekly) and recess (one 30-minute session daily)
target_learning_goals: mathematics fluency
reading fluency
increased school-day physical activity
examples: Pedometers (Walk4Life LS 2500) were worn five consecutive school days at baseline and one random day per week during the intervention to measure school-day PA

article_title: Enhancing Learners' Problem Solving Performance in Mathematics: A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Dhlamini, J. J. (2016). Enhancing learners’ problem solving performance in mathematics: A cognitive load perspective. European Journal of STEM Education, 1(1), 27-36. https://doi.org/10.20897/lectito.201604
title: Cognitive load theory as a framework for modelling problem solving performance
description: The article frames problem solving performance within cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988), which holds that working memory has severely limited processing capacity and duration when dealing with novel information, while long-term memory stores unlimited schemas that reduce mental effort. The paper distinguishes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load, arguing the three are additive and overload occurs when their sum exceeds working memory capacity. It presents a conceptual diagram (Figure 1) illustrating techniques to manipulate cognitive load to foster learning and problem solving performance, which guided the design of CBPSI.
requirements: Instruction should minimize extraneous load and optimize germane load by keeping intrinsic and extraneous loads at manageable levels
constraints: The framework applies the limitations of working memory only to new, yet-to-be-learned information; well-learned material in long-term memory suffers neither limitation
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving performance in financial mathematics
examples: The pilot study applied CLT by using worked-out examples, physically integrating problem elements to reduce split-attention, and grounding tasks in learners' everyday experiences

article_title: Clinical Supervision Model in Teaching Practice: Does It Make a Difference in Supervisors' Performance?
citation: Gürsoy, E., Kesner, J. E., & Salihoglu, U. M. (2016). Clinical Supervision Model in Teaching Practice: Does it Make a Difference in Supervisors' Performance?. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 41(11). https://doi.org/10.14221/ajte.2016v41n11.5
title: Clinical Supervision Model (CSM) for teaching practice
description: The CSM is a collaborative supervision program involving the teacher trainee, cooperating teacher, and university supervisor, adapted from a model used at a major university in the southeastern United States. The article states that "the CT and US observe and provide systematic feedback to the TT, and opportunities for TT self-reflection in an effort to improve the TTs' performance in the classroom." Stakeholders receive training in observation techniques, feedback language, three-way conferences, data collection, reflective techniques, and action plans, with coordinators maintaining communication to strengthen the triadic relationship.
requirements: Training for CTs and USs in their roles, observation techniques, feedback language, three-way conferences, and reflective techniques
Communication between stakeholders maintained through coordinators throughout the teaching practice
constraints: Evaluated in one large Turkish state university's classroom teacher training program; the article notes results come from "this one teacher education program"
target_learners: preservice teacher trainees (TTs) in teaching practice
target_learning_goals: improving teaching performance through systematic observation, feedback, and self-reflection
examples: Experimental-group CTs and USs were trained in CSM techniques and implemented them over two academic years, compared with a control group following the procedural-only Faculty-School Cooperation Manual

article_title: Preschoolers' Alphabet Learning: Letter Name and Sound Instruction, Cognitive Processes, and English Proficiency
citation: Theresa A. Roberts, Patricia F. Vadasy, Elizabeth A. Sanders. (2018). Preschoolers' Alphabet Learning: Letter Name and Sound Instruction, Cognitive Processes, and English Proficiency. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2018.04.011
title: Alphabet learning as visual-verbal paired-associate learning supported by articulation-referencing and orthographic learning subcomponents
description: The article conceptualizes alphabet learning as drawing primarily on "visual-verbal paired associate learning (PAL)" — forming associations between printed letter forms and verbal labels. Two subcomponents are targeted separately: articulation-referencing learning (ARL), an instructional routine based on speech articulation targeting the verbal component, and orthographic learning (OL), a writing-based routine targeting the visual component. The framework holds that "highly effective instruction explicitly engages the primary learning processes involved in learning alphabet content" and that engagement is a function of cognitive and affective constructs supported through attention deployment and participation routines.
requirements: Instructional routines must exercise the verbal and visual components of PAL individually as well as jointly
constraints: Task difficulty increases when names and sounds are taught together because more associations must be learned and names and sounds are confusable for young children
target_learning_goals: letter identification accuracy and speed
letter-sound and letter-name association learning
examples: ARL routines used photographs of children's mouth shapes forming letter sounds; OL routines used letter writing from memory to build cross-modal links between spelling and sound

article_title: Concentrated Language Encounter Approach in Practice for Global Teaching of Literacy: Lighthouse Strategy Implementation
citation: Rattanavich, S. (2015). Concentrated Language Encounter Approach in Practice for Global Teaching of Literacy: Lighthouse Strategy Implementation. International Education Studies, 8(7), 21. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n7p21
title: Concentrated Language Encounter (CLE) approach: staged lesson sequences producing target texts through scaffolding, routines, and teacher-student negotiation
description: The CLE approach, developed by Gray at Traeger Park and defined as "a sequence of lessons that focused upon the production of a specific text," teaches language through texts chosen for their social function, with the teacher pre-analyzing the language resources needed. Lessons are staged as "routines" in which the same text is revisited over time with expanding scope, grounded in Vygotskyan scaffolding where teachers let children do as much as they can and gradually hand over control. Two lesson-sequence types are distinguished: Type A encounters produce written texts from shared experiences, and Type B encounters derive from experiences with texts read to, with, or by students. The article stresses CLE is experiential but differs from child-centered whole-language approaches in the strength of the adult role and the acceptance of imitation.
requirements: Teachers analyze and define the language contextual resources necessary for producing the target text prior to teaching
Lesson sequences must be staged as routines with repeated revisiting of the same text over time
Both teachers and children take an active part in negotiating the children's learning
constraints: The article states it is misleading to presume an affinity with child-centered language experience approaches such as whole language, despite the experiential character of CLE
target_learning_goals: literacy in Thai and English
control of a range of text types and genres
spoken, written, and nonverbal communication
examples: Gray's Type A example: making toast together at school entry as the basis for children gaining control over an extended procedural text
A CLE lesson sequence on saddling a horse within a broader cattle-station theme at Traeger Park

article_title: Concentrated Language Encounter Approach in Practice for Global Teaching of Literacy: Lighthouse Strategy Implementation
citation: Rattanavich, S. (2015). Concentrated Language Encounter Approach in Practice for Global Teaching of Literacy: Lighthouse Strategy Implementation. International Education Studies, 8(7), 21. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n7p21
title: Three CLE stages/models of literacy development paired with four program types (formal, informal, special education, ethnic group)
description: The Thai CLE program organizes literacy teaching around three stages: stage 1 for beginner readers aims to create enthusiasm for reading and writing simple texts; stage 2 widens the range of text types learners can read and write independently; stage 3 for advanced learners emphasizes learning through reading and writing and the literacy skills needed after school. The article states "The CLE programs were also categorized into four types of literacy programs": formal or school-based, informal education (adult literacy and children), special education for disabled students, and ethnic group programs for hill tribe students and immigrants. Each stage specifies phases of instruction in text-based and activity-based units (Table 1) and a taxonomy of target genres increasing in complexity.
requirements: Curriculum development, key personnel training, material development, and research studies organized per program type
Genre-based (text-based) planning of beginner texts with teachers trained in linguistic inquiry into genres and schematic structure
constraints: When the program spread to other regions of Thailand, some curriculum themes had to be replaced due to geographical and sociocultural differences
target_learning_goals: reading and writing across transactional, factual, and literary text types
Thai and English language communicative performance
learning-to-learn and enjoyment of literacy
examples: Stage 1 texts include story books, procedural 'how to' books, expository information books, and incidental letters and notices
Stage 3 texts include scientific reports, plays and films, radio scripts, commercial and public documents, and reference books

Item editing on the web with mandatory or optional answers specified

examples: Test-takers saw the correct answer for each item after confirming the question, and a certification appeared on screen at 70 or higher points

article_title: Enhancing Expectations of Cooperative Learning Use through Initial Teacher Training
citation: Duran, D; Corcelles, M. & Flores, M. (2017). Enhancing Expectations of Cooperative Learning Use through Initial Teacher Training. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(3), 278-300. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2017.2504
title: CLIQ three-factor model of cooperative learning implementation (value, expectancy, cost)
description: The CLIQ questionnaire is based on three factors that predict teachers' implementation of cooperative learning. The article describes that "Value items assess to what extent teachers perceive CL as beneficial", "Expectancy items explore the teachers' perceptions concerning CL use and expected results", and "cost items assess perceptions of the physical and psychological cost of CL use". A weighted formula combines them: (0.44 × expectancy) + (0.04 × value) − (0.01 × cost) = Index of cooperative learning use, accounting for more than 40% of variance in regular CL use.

constraints: The model was derived from responses of more than 1000 teachers and its weights are specific to that dataset

examples: The article applied CLIQ pre- and post-test with 89 pre-service teachers

article_title: Using Computers in Relation to Learning Climate in CLIL Method
citation: Helena Binterová, Olga Komínková. (2013). Using Computers in Relation to Learning Climate in CLIL Method. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 6, Number 1, 2013.
title: CLIL as an integrative approach developing content and language through a mutual relation.
description: CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) refers to teaching a non-language subject using a foreign language, which serves as a means of communication and content sharing. Non-language content is mediated and developed using a foreign language while the foreign language is developed by mediating the content, so that both are developed through a mutual relation. The term was coined in 1994 and first used in 1996, and is referred to by many authors as an "umbrella term" including a number of different approaches in different educational contexts.
requirements: Teachers must take into account the cognitive development of students so that lower-level mental operations are followed by higher-level ones.
constraints: Risks include students' inability to use a foreign language in special subjects, a lack of relevant learning materials, and insufficient language or subject skills of the teachers.
target_learners: Primary and secondary school pupils learning non-language subjects through a foreign language
target_learning_goals: Developing both content knowledge and foreign language skills simultaneously
examples: The project 'Connecting Foreign Languages and School Subjects at Primary Schools' implemented CLIL into primary school Mathematics teaching at least once or twice a week.

article_title: Edmodo Use to Develop Saudi EFL Students' Self-Directed Learning
citation: Khodary, M. M. (2017). Edmodo Use to Develop Saudi EFL Students' Self-Directed Learning. English Language Teaching, 10(2), 123. http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n2p123
title: Use a closed, secure social learning network such as Edmodo to give students a safe, private setting for self-directed learning activities.
description: Edmodo is a closed social learning network considered unique compared to other SNSs because it gives a safe, private setting to users; each student has a private access code provided by the teacher and no strangers can join it. The researcher concluded that this characteristic helped the participants feel safe and hence they had great interest in the task because they realized that no strangers can see their own comments or comment on their own work.
requirements: The platform must be private and closed for only educational uses by its users, with teacher-controlled registration via private access codes.
Students must be trained on how to log on and use the platform individually and collaboratively before carrying out project requirements.
constraints: Edmodo use is still rare in KSA universities, and the researcher did not find any studies conducted on its effects on developing SDL among university students in KSA prior to this study.
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
online collaboration and communication
examples: The researcher created a class Edmodo for the Research Methods course, made an account on Edmodo for each participant and provided each one with her own password and username on Edmodo to privately and safely use it.

constraints: CLIL shares elements with bilingual education and immersion but is not synonymous with them

additional language competence
examples: Secciones bilingües in Galician primary schools, where at least one subject is taught through CLIL

description: The Concentrated Language Encounter approach holds that children learn language mainly through encounters with others in which they concentrate intensely on making themselves understood. The article identifies three principles: "an immersion program in which children are constantly involved in doing new and ever more challenging activities using language"; scaffolding, where the teacher models and supports what students need to accomplish; and activity-based learning in which students understand the meaning of what they read and write. The approach draws on the natural approach, genre-based approach, and communicative approach.

description: CLE Model III is a structured instructional sequence that "begins with a reading stage and continues through a writing task stage systematically." article_title: Input structure-driven instability and convergence in large language model clinical reasoning: a formative study using pediatric residency-level MCQs.
citation: Vinson, J., Caronia, C., & Savargaonkar, R. (2026). Input structure–driven instability and convergence in large language model clinical reasoning: a formative study using pediatric residency–level MCQs. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-48326-4
title: Cognitive Load Theory and assessment theory as a conceptual framework for LLM input-structure instability
description: The study integrates Cognitive Load Theory and assessment theory within a clarification-oriented educational research framework to explain why LLM clinical reasoning varies with delivery format. Cognitive Load Theory holds that "learning and performance deteriorate when the cognitive demands of a task exceed the processing capacity of working memory," and assessment theory holds that discrete itemized questions minimize "construct-irrelevant variance." The authors hypothesized that simultaneous delivery amplifies inter-model variability while structured sequential delivery stabilizes performance, positioning prompt structure as a mechanistic determinant of LLM reliability. They explicitly frame the cognitive load analogy as a useful pedagogical metaphor rather than a claim of mechanistic equivalence.
requirements: Structured batch delivery aligned with cognitive load management and assessment design principles
constraints: The cognitive load analogy is a pedagogical metaphor, not a claim of mechanistic equivalence between transformer attention and human working memory
target_learners: medical trainees preparing for USMLE Step 2/3
target_learning_goals: clinical diagnostic reasoning
management decision-making
ethical judgment

title: The CLM Competency Model of four supra-competencies (Conceptualise, Align, Interact, Create Success)

description: The article uses Cognitive Load Theory as its theoretical frame for why low-stakes testing works: "Low‐stakes testing aligns with CLT's principles by reducing extraneous load (ungraded assessments mitigate stress, which can deplete working memory) and promoting germane processing (active recall strengthens knowledge construction and long‐term memory integration)." Instructional content presented in a structured, sequential manner for novice learners

For more experienced learners, methods effective for novices may lose efficacy or hinder learning (expertise reversal effect)

citation: Su, Dongying; Meijuan, Gai; Aikebaier, Simayilijiang. (2026). Cognitive load and teachers' innovative behavior in AI-enhanced English language instruction: A mediation analysis of technological adaptability. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0343002
title: Integrated CLT–TAM–IDT framework with technological adaptability as mediator
description: The article develops a theoretical framework synthesizing Cognitive Load Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Innovation Diffusion Theory to explain how cognitive demands influence teaching innovation through adaptive mechanisms. As the article states, it integrates these theories "through three theoretical mechanisms: distributed cognition, cognitive offloading, and adaptive scaffolding," depicting technological adaptability as a mediator between cognitive load and innovative teaching behavior with hypotheses H1a, H1b, and H1c. Distributed cognition reconceptualizes cognitive load as a dynamically negotiated phenomenon spanning human and technological agents, while cognitive offloading describes how educators strategically externalize cognitive functions onto AI systems.
requirements: Technological adaptability functioning as the mediating construct linking internal cognitive constraints to observable innovation patterns
constraints: The framework was tested with a cross-sectional design, which the authors state cannot capture developmental trajectories across AI implementation stages

target_learning_goals: Understanding how cognitive demands influence pedagogical innovation in AI-enhanced teaching

title: Cognitive load theory as the explanatory account for the procedural-skill advantage of live-video demonstration
description: The article applies cognitive load theory, under which learning is most effective when design manages working-memory limits and instructional design aims "to minimize extraneous load to free up cognitive resources". Traditional at-the-chairside teaching imposes extraneous load through obstructed viewing angles, non-repeatable demonstrations, and abstract verbal explanation; the 4K camera provides "a multi-angle and unobstructed view" from the instructor's co-axial line of sight, transforming abstract demonstrations into concrete experiences and freeing resources for germane schema building. The authors use this account to explain the procedural-skills and EPA gains in their trial.
requirements: Procedures of high intrinsic complexity (e.g., tooth extraction) where visual access to the operative field otherwise forces mental reconstruction
constraints: Applied in a preclinical simulated setting with a manikin; the article presents this as an interpretation of the results, not a directly measured load
target_learners: Fifth-year undergraduate dental students preparing for OMFS clinical internships
target_learning_goals: Foundational oral surgery procedural skills and EPA-related competencies
examples: A miniature 4K camera was mounted on the instructor's operating light handle, broadcasting a fixed co-axial feed to 18 monitors, with recordings archived and replayed in post-session debriefing

title: Closed-loop blended model aligning MOOC theoretical preparation with virtual simulation deliberate practice, framed by Kolb's experiential learning theory

title: Three-phase clinical simulation framework: preparation, participation and debriefing
description: The review describes clinical simulation in health as an educational strategy that exposes participants to hypothetical scenarios mimicking clinical practice, structured in three phases. In its words, "its phases, called preparation, participation and debriefing, must be conceptualized and understood". Preparation is divided into pre-simulation (educational materials and skills training) and pre-briefing/briefing (facilitator-participant interaction with clear scenarios, objectives and learning roles); participation involves carrying out the proposed scenario; debriefing is a discussion/reflection process during or after the scenario. The review applies this framework to caregiver training for hospital discharge, arguing that simulation "planned and executed in three stages enables the teaching and learning process of complex subjects".
requirements: Preparation phase must be conceptualized and understood, including delivery of educational materials and skills training before the scenario
Debriefing must occur during or after the scenario as a discussion/reflection process
constraints: The article notes financial, structural and organizational challenges, including caregivers' literacy level and their emotional and affective states, which influence learning

target_learning_goals: Technical care skills (e.g., tracheostomy, oxygen therapy, drainage management) and non-technical skills such as confidence, decision-making and managing anxiety for home care
examples: A5 implemented a multimodal discharge readiness curriculum with high-fidelity simulation in which post-simulation debriefing was reported as the most beneficial component

title: Increase case-based (clinical vignette) questions to maintain MCQ discriminative power in high-scoring groups
description: This principle holds that when an MCQ exam serves academically heterogeneous groups, adding questions based on clinical vignettes helps preserve discriminative power where factual questions lose it. The article states the lower discriminative power in high-scoring groups "could be attenuated increasing the number of case-based questions", because case-based questions explore reasoning across situations rather than only recall. constraints: The study was retrospective, in a single School of Medicine with few teachers generating the MCQ, and the proportion of vignette questions was low

target_learning_goals: assessment discrimination between students of different academic performance levels
examples: In the studied pathophysiology exams, 59 of 257 questions were case-based and maintained similar discrimination indices in both student groups while factual questions did not

Anxiety is associated with extraneous cognitive load during teaching using high-fidelity clinical simulation. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.1994691
title: Cognitive load theory's three-component framework, with germane load reinterpreted as self-perceived learning, applied to simulation
description: The article applies cognitive load theory to simulation teaching: working memory capacity is fixed and learning is hindered when it is overloaded. Three components contribute to total load: "the intrinsic cognitive load (ICL) of the learning task itself, the extraneous cognitive load (ECL) of the actual learning situation, and the germane cognitive load or self-perceived learning (SPL)". Germane load is reinterpreted as self-perceived learning via the Leppink CLS, and the framework guides instructional design by distinguishing task-inherent load from load imposed by non-essential context elements such as anxiety-generated thoughts.
requirements: Measured with a validated subjective instrument (Leppink CLS) distinguishing the three components
constraints: Germane cognitive load is described as more controversial than ICL and ECL
Few published studies report CL components in relation to simulation; research has focused on total CL
target_learning_goals: Clinical competencies such as history taking, examination, investigation, management and communication in emergency scenarios
examples: The study used the 13-item CLS with ICL, ECL and SPL subscales after simulation scenarios to test which components relate to state-anxiety

teamwork and team-role awareness
